Focus on the what, who and why, and not on the how!! https://t.co/O3cjhVuuP1

As these network attacks and impersonation attempts happen, who's securing the elderly? 

Especially thinking about my parents and grandparents.

There are four layers I can think through where this could work.

One is at the browser level, where somebody builds a secure browser that ensures that whatever websites they're going to are secured. Texts typically lead to a link, even for payments. This is why browser is key.

Two could be at the network layer, where there is a physical device, similar to Pi-hole, or an Onavo-like VPN on your phone, that blocks websites that could be deemed unsafe.

Three could be at the payments layer, where transactions that look like scams get flagged before the money leaves.

And fourth and most crazy could be at the phone level, where everything is monitored, and you're only getting calls from your loved ones. Cloned voices would work with a provider like Reality Defender. 

There are individual solutions for this today but none neatly packaged. 

This could all be packaged with insurance that covers any activities on the OS or phone. In that way, incentives are aligned to keep this on the edge.

The buyer would be the kids, someone like me, who get alerted when something looks off.

It is very important for crypto people to read this analysis by @BoringBiz_.

I said back in May that most of the crypto industry was dead and it was never coming back. I believe that even more today.

Where I disagree with @BoringBiz_ is that these four areas of crypto seem to be resilient and value-creating: 

1. Bitcoin
2. Stablecoins (Tether, etc)
3. Infrastructure (Coinbase, Binance, etc)
4. Tokenization (Figure, Hyperliquid, etc)

Everything else in crypto is going to have a very tough time going forward. 

Additionally, it is clear that AI has produced enormous benefits for hundreds of millions of people around the world. The companies are producing impressive revenue growth, while continuing to heavily invest in future acceleration. 

The smartest crypto investors I know have expanded their focus area from exclusively "crypto" to a broader "frontier technologies" or "crypto and AI."

I literally run one of the only public companies that sits at the intersection of bitcoin and AI (@cfosilvia).

It is a sign of intelligence to change your mind, or evolve your thinking, when the facts change.

I remain bullish on bitcoin, but there are a lot of ways up the mountain too...

Give @BoringBiz_ a follow while you are at it.

"American power exists because America has men who make it exist; through their courage, their competence, and their guts. These men take on and carry out work that is technically difficult and existentially costly. Work that some never come home from, and that often leaves a mark on the ones who do. Before a nation can have a republic, an empire, or become a globe-spanning hegemony, it must have a special type of man. All of our grand strategy and statecraft rest entirely on their shoulders."

Read this: https://t.co/LxA91j2jH2

There are two tales to Anthropic's story.

On one hand, the company's financial performance is incredible. They did over $16 billion in revenue in Q3. This was nearly 4x higher than all revenue in 2025.

The speed and scale of the financials is very impressive.

At the same time, there is widespread mistrust of Anthropic. The whole "AI safety" approach comes off as inauthentic and it scares people when the leaders of the company keep trying to claim the moral high ground. 

I could argue that mistrust will create headwinds for any business over time, but the financials tell us that the market has such high demand for intelligence that it doesn't matter at the moment.

The big question is how competition will play into the future value of Anthropic. 

They are under constant attack from OpenAI, Google, SpaceX, and many others for generalized intelligence. There is also immense competition in specific verticals from specialized workflow companies that are trying to win individual categories. 

All boats can rise together. But also, competition is for losers. 

I would expect a short-term pop in Anthropic's stock price today, followed by volatility as the market tries to figure out what the company is actually worth long-term.

tweets.text: Everyone ready for December 15th #Midnight $NIGHT @SebastienGllmt https://t.co/en5dtLIWIa

For those interested in the AMA, I had my agents transcribe it: 

1. What is working on Cardano, and what is not?
Gregaard said node diversity is working: the Haskell node, plus Amaru, Dingo, and Bean, are producing mainnet blocks; Tsunag was also checked, and the London node-diversity workshop showed the teams cooperating. CIP-113 programmable tokens are on mainnet, so blacklist and whitelist rules can sit in the native asset. That, plus Fireblocks, expected at the end of Q1, is what he thinks makes tokenization on Cardano competitive for traditional finance and DeFi. He also cited uptime, stake pool operators, the security council, and partnerships including Petrobras, DFX Bar, the Syngenta Foundation, Trivolve, and Blockforce. Blockforce keeps business logic on Hyperledger and uses Cardano as the trust and reporting layer to regulators. Midnight is the full-privacy partner chain. Separate projects offer selective disclosure on Cardano itself, hiding amounts and metadata while addresses stay visible. What is not working is commercialization. The chain is built, but the ecosystem still lacks a shared commercial roadmap and a budget aimed at adoption.

2. Where does Midnight fit, after it was left out of Gregaard's Sunday post?
The Foundation now focuses on the top 20 projects on the https://t.co/pAsp5blYs8 leaderboard and on who could join that list. Night was around 7th or 8th by transactions over the last 30 days, so the Cardano-native Night asset is in scope. The Foundation has helped with exchange listings and press. Night counts toward Cardano TVL. Activity on the partner chain is separate, and Midnight mainnet is still early. He also tied this to a wider opening: permissioned chains such as Hyperledger and R3 Corda built use cases that didn't pay off, and those clients and code can move to Cardano, with Midnight as the full-privacy option.

3. Catalyst went from 12 selected teams to 7. What is the transition, and what comes next?
Andreas Pletscher said the Foundation brought in the Catalyst team earlier this year. The first job was to finish funding the community had already selected. The team is now five people. The new pilot pays for adoption rather than promises. Community panels and the Foundation cut the field to 12, then onboarding diligence dropped it to 7 because some teams could not yet deliver what they had described. Those teams were told to come back later. The seven-project pilot is running now. A proposal for the next cycles is aimed at early 2027: sound it out with the community first, then withdraw from the treasury if there is agreement.

4. What is the builder path, and where do the Academy, accelerators, and enterprise work sit?
Stephen Wood said founders keep asking why build on Cardano and what support exists. The path they joined up this year is learn, build, accelerate, scale. Learn is the Cardano Academy plus university courses. Build is Catalyst. Accelerate is four programs the Foundation runs or supports: its own accelerator (8 ventures), Draper (8), the UNDP SDG blockchain accelerator (4, starting soon), and UCLA in 2027 (5). Scale is an enterprise program that takes an organization from a first conversation to a pilot. A few of those are under NDA, with announcements toward the end of 2026 or in 2027.

5. As the original roadmap nears completion, how is the Foundation's mandate changing, and how do you measure success?
Gregaard said Emurgo's original job was commercialization and IOG's was building the first version of the protocol. The Foundation is different. Its Swiss deed is to promote third-generation blockchains such as Cardano, including regulation and policy, on a long horizon because it is not-for-profit. He measures three jobs. Operational resilience: the chain still exists in 10, 20, and 30 years. Policy: they filed on the MiCA consultation and work with regulators, so Cardano use is faster, better, and cheaper than the old system, with proof points in jobs and GDP. He highlighted India, two Trivolve projects (a police station and grain track-and-trace), and a Syngenta program he put in place for close to 200,000 farmers, providing identity, education, and access to digital finance via low-orbit satellites. Enabling adoption meant standards, token models, language choice, CIP-113 payment rails, and Aiken being accepted on GitHub as a language. He said Emurgo is winding down while repaying people hit by its hack, and IOG is moving to building on Cardano, which leaves a gap in who coordinates adoption. The Foundation tried building products years ago, but they did not generate revenue. It is now using the venture hub, accelerators, and outside capital such as Draper. Inside the Foundation, automation is being used to make the organization leaner and to move the saved people into commercialization. He was explicit that the Foundation alone cannot make Cardano economically self-sustaining.

6. What does the Foundation do that people do not see, and is it doing and spending enough?
Gregaard pointed to the yearly activity report, https://t.co/LJwVRK4Beh, and https://t.co/pAsp5blYs8. Policy conversations with regulators often cannot be published. The Foundation has been market-making: an eight-figure amount of ADA into DeFi, active market-making in stablecoins that cut slippage by more than half, and CME futures, where it helped get the listing and is about to market-make. The burn rate is about 27 to 28 million Swiss francs a year, for nearly 109 people. His test for new executives is whether the impact is at least double the spend. He said some bets failed, and some landed that other chains do not have, including the India deployments. DeFi was a focus of the past year, including work with Alpha Growth, and he said they found structural problems in Cardano DeFi that they are trying to fix with people already in the community.

7. Why should the 2027 global events proposal, 12 events, come from the treasury instead of the Foundation?
Wood said this is not the first time. The 2025 global marketing report, with an auditor's attestation, is planned for Reeve before year-end. The Foundation already spends on its own marketing and is putting staff time into this proposal, which he estimated at over $600,000. The booth is Cardano-branded and shared with projects, so he called it ecosystem work, which is what the treasury is for. DReps approved the same model for 2025 with nearly 70% support. Pletscher, who was at the Nairobi event, said the lesson from last year was that 12 events is the compromise between "be everywhere" and a real calendar. The Foundation organizes them and does not make money on them. He said one other layer-1 spent about the same at Token2049 in Singapore as this proposal spends on all 12 events, so he thinks Cardano is not spending enough. Industry-specific events beyond the 12 are paid for from the Foundation's own funds.

8. How can the community hold the Foundation accountable?
Gregaard said the founders put the Foundation under Swiss law, so the board and executives have unlimited personal liability for the deed. Every transaction is posted on-chain, with context files. The budget and the year's plan go to an external board, measured against a 10-year strategy he said was checked with Ken Kodama and Charles Hoskinson. The original allocation was meant to last about five years. They are close to ten and still paying salaries. On Veridian, he said they refused the easy path of a treasury withdrawal and instead raised outside money. Any revenue has to come back to the Foundation and, under the deed, be spent promoting third-generation blockchains.

9. What can people actually see in Reeve, and how do the audits work?
Wood said he did his own homework in the interview by reading Reeve's transaction-level data. Figures are published quarterly. Getting the accounts from the accounting system onto the chain through Reeve takes about four hours a quarter. Audited statements are moving from once a year to every six months, which is not legally required. An outsider can check the statements every half year. Seeing every transaction on-chain is what he called unusual.

10. What does the Fireblocks integration unlock, and who uses it?
Gregaard said Fireblocks is how DeFi rails meet institutional custody. He estimated Fireblocks at about 80% of large institutional players. Talks went on for years. A deal was on the table and died with the Pentad. Phil at Emurgo reopened it, and the Foundation signed. It opens roughly 70 to 80% of the institutional custodian market, which he said does little until there is issuance on Cardano. Fireblocks wants a joint go-to-market with the Foundation's sales team and the community.

11. As IOG work moves to new companies, what is the Foundation's role?
Nicolas named Blockpqr, ICAN, and Midgard-type labs as the teams taking on maintenance. Gregaard said IOG is still the best at building chains, and these new teams should be the resilience and maintenance layer, with future features funded through Intersect committees. He wants the node teams to stay in sync, and he wants to flip the order of words: commercial or user need first, then research, then engineering, for retail, B2B, and B2B2C. "More users" was the point, not only large enterprises.

Open floor

12. Jonah Koch: Will the Foundation open offices beyond Europe, in places like New York, San Francisco, Tokyo, and Latin America, now that the other founding entities have stepped back?
Gregaard said the current offices are administrative, not sales offices. Swiss incorporation requires a real presence there. The old split was IOG covering the US and Emurgo covering Asia. He doesn't think a thousand-person sales force, paid from the Foundation or through repeated treasury withdrawals, would scale. They have two people in Brazil, no staff physically in India, and rely on local teams there, including Rahul's group and Joram's. He expects more Foundation salespeople in more countries, and said they are not Europe-only. He also said Europe may lead in regulatory use over the next three to five years without leading in transaction count.

13. Jonah, follow-up: Can the Foundation carry Europe's regulatory approach into the US and other countries?
Yes, and he said they already do. Three people were on stage this week at a state digital-identity conference in Utah and spoke with more than 20 state policymakers. He said Foundation work around privacy, children, and guardianship, using the KERI standard, was part of a change to the Utah constitution and a state digital-identity effort. He has also been on Capitol Hill with agriculture and commodities staff, and the legal team has advised and co-written digital-asset rules for some African countries. They cannot cover every country. The US has to be covered.

14. Jenny Brito: Cardano, Midnight, Veridian, and other projects each have ambassadors, and the argument is whether Midnight or spinning Veridian out helps Cardano. How do those ambassadors collaborate, including people who arrived through Midnight and do not know Cardano?
Gregaard said this is the real problem with a global sales force that doesn't take orders from one entity. His three pieces of advice were: use the Cardano Academy, including the track where a non-engineer uses an AI agent to try a business idea on Cardano; start from a real business problem (cost, retention, or a smoother operation), not from another chain's feature list; and stop treating chains as mutually exclusive, because Cardano's research already shaped other chains and the design goal was interoperability. Jenny proposed reciprocal Academy sessions for Midnight and Cardano ambassadors. He agreed and said he would aim first at Hyperledger and R3 Corda ambassadors, because their business logic can move to Cardano quickly. She wanted the existing programs to try it too. Nicolas said he would take it to Sebastian, who runs the ambassador program.

Close

15. Ten years out, what does a successful Cardano look like, and what is the Foundation's role in getting there?
Gregaard said the Foundation was never meant to last forever. The original budget was about five years; they will be out of money within ten years, and the job now is to fill blocks. For him, success is two things: the chain actually changes financial and social systems, and it is economically self-sustaining. There aren't enough transactions, and they aren't the right mix. Bot-to-bot trading does not count. Fee income has to cover stake pool operators, delegators, and ongoing research. Until then, ADA stays under pressure from the market, treasury withdrawals, and low transaction volume

Wood said he is doing that math inside Cardano's parameters, and that a year in the job has been as much about learning from the community as from the Foundation, including project teams who came up to him at Token2049 in Singapore.

Pletscher said success is Cardano as critical infrastructure inside industries, bridging or replacing old systems. They are closer to the operational assurance enterprises need, and not there yet. The second half is the community. He said the Foundation expects to be yelled at when something is wrong. He asked that DeFi, traditional finance, liquidity, security, and live projects be treated as one system. Security doesn't get traded away, and liquidity has to come from both inside and outside.

Nicolas closed by thanking Jonah, Jenny, a nd everyone who posted questions on the announcement post. Only Jonah and Jenny were brought on stage. The written replies on that post were not read out and answered one by one.

德鲁肯米勒（Stanley Druckenmiller）最近在一期新访谈里说：“做投资整整 50 年，我几乎记不清什么时候我对未来一年的方向能像现在这样毫无头绪。我现在每天的状态就是自动回复：别来找我，我选择不入局。”

这位做过索罗斯操盘手、30 年几乎没有年度亏损的大佬@standuquesne，在加密圈其实并不陌生。之前纽交所母公司 ICE 战略投资 https://t.co/iIrXOmWVhW、计划把 Hyperliquid 合约带入美国的时候，他也参与了投资，很多玩家都熟悉他那套“先上车，再研究”（Buy first, analyze later）的激进风格。

但就是这样一个向来敢下注的老操盘手，这次在访谈里却把仓位全清了，顺便还戳破了自己身上最出名的“不败神话”。

30 年不亏钱很大程度纯属日历运气。他年中一样挨过惨烈的回撤，只是运气好，每次都能在 12 月底关账前把坑填平。做投资别去迷信什么神准择时。

他说自己从来不死守股票。过去股市行情烂的时候，往往外汇、美债和商品正在走出大趋势，在多资产之间切换才是宏观对冲的意义。

但眼下的问题在于，股市估值偏高，债市和外汇也全是一团迷雾，所有大类资产的逻辑全都看不懂了。

用他的话说，既然完全看不清球路，那索性就不挥杆。

在大机会面前“先上车再研究”，在全市场迷雾时“彻底不入局”。看似矛盾，但其实都是老操盘手能活过 50 年的生存法则：看不懂的时候，管住手不亏钱，就是最大的赢面。

A家上市，链上目前还是延续了看多情绪和抢筹心理。

https://t.co/iIrXOmXt7u 上 $ANT 合约较 IPO 发行价溢价约 25% 左右，来到了103美元附近。

而Anthropic 将 IPO 发行价定为每股 83 美元，高于此前 70 至 78 美元的指导区间。

两者之间接近 20 美元的价差，说明一级市场留出了较厚的安全垫，市场普遍预期上市首日会有可观的“首日涨幅（IPO Pop）”。

此外，在美股半导体与 AI 板块因担忧算力资本开支放缓而经历回调的背景下，Anthropic 的高定价似乎还起到了“强心剂”作用。

盘前及上市前夕，Alphabet 与美光科技股价均涨超 4%，AMD、英伟达、博通、英特尔以及存储板块如闪迪等全线走强，纳斯达克 100 期货同步走高。
